CVE-2026-60008.title: Jupyter notebook renderer emits attacker-controlled CSS classes into unsanitized, unsandboxed output
CVE-2026-60008.description: `modules/markup/jupyter/jupyter.go` sets `SanitizerDisabled: true` but leaves `DisplayInIframe` and `ContentSandbox` at their zero values. It is the only renderer in the tree that turns the sanitizer off while still rendering into the main document. Within that unsanitized output it interpolates `notebook.metadata.language_info.name` — a value read directly from the file — into a literal `class` attribute without routing it through `RenderInternal.FormatWithSafeAttrs`. HTML-escaping prevents closing the attribute, but whitespace is untouched, so the notebook can choose its own list of CSS classes on a page where nothing filters them. Combined with Fomantic's `.ui.dimmer` and Gitea's `!important` Tailwind layer, a repository file can replace the entire viewport of a repository page and intercept clicks on it. Script execution was not reached. The reason to fix this is not the overlay: it is that the class attribute is the one place on this path where a security control was skipped, and there is no sanitizer, no iframe sandbox and no CSP behind it. ## Why this is a boundary failure rather than a cosmetic bug Gitea has a deliberate mechanism to stop rendered content from choosing CSS classes. `RenderInternal.ProtectSafeAttrs` rewrites `class='X'` into `data-attr-class='<per-render-nonce>:X'`; the sanitizer allows `data-attr-class`; and `finalProcessor.Close` converts it back only when the nonce matches. Content cannot forge the nonce, so only the renderer's own trusted code can emit a class. `orgmode.go` uses this correctly: ```go _ = ctx.RenderInternal.FormatWithSafeAttrs(sb, `<pre><code class='chroma language-%s'>`, ...) ``` The intent is also written down inside the affected file itself, in the `text/html` MIME handler: ```go // To future developers: don't allow custom CSS classes or attributes, // because '.link-action' or 'data-fetch-xxx' can send POST requests and lead to XSS. ``` That rule is enforced for MIME output and missed for the language field. ## Details **1. The sanitizer is disabled and the output is not confined.** ```go func (renderer) GetExternalRendererOptions() markup.ExternalRendererOptions { return markup.ExternalRendererOptions{ SanitizerDisabled: true, } } ``` `DisplayInIframe` and `ContentSandbox` are left unset. In `modules/markup/render.go` that removes `SanitizeReader` from the pipeline, and the bytes land inside `<div class='file-view markup jupyter-render'>` on the ordinary repository page. By contrast the `openapi-swagger`, `viewer-3d` and `asciicast` renderers also disable the sanitizer, but set `DisplayInIframe: true` and `ContentSandbox: setting.MarkupRenderDefaultSandbox`, so their output is confined to an iframe with no `allow-same-origin`. **2. Untrusted input reaches a literal `class` attribute.** The `language` value comes from `notebook.metadata.language_info.name`, falling back to `metadata.kernelspec.language`, and is interpolated into a `class='chroma language-…'` attribute. `htmlutil.WriteFormat` applies `template.HTMLEscapeString`, which handles `< > & ' '` and leaves whitespace alone. No input yields a raw `'`, so no new attribute can be created — but spaces pass through, which is enough to append arbitrary additional CSS classes. **3. `/render/` serves the same content with no CSP.** The `/render/` route adds a `Content-Security-Policy: sandbox …` header only when the renderer sets `ContentSandbox`, a field the Jupyter renderer never sets. The result is a top-level, same-origin, navigable `text/html` document built from repository content, with the sanitizer off and no restrictions, reachable anonymously on public repositories. Repository authorization on the route itself is sound (private repositories return 404 to unauthorized users). **4. The notebook selects which frontend renderer processes it.** Because the class is built as `language-%s` from the file, a notebook can declare `'language_info': {'name': 'mermaid'}` (or `math`) and hand its cell source to mermaid.js / KaTeX. Those frontend paths assign markup via `innerHTML` in the parent document before moving it into a non-sandboxed iframe. Today mermaid's `securityLevel: 'strict'` and KaTeX's `trust: false` hold, so script execution was not achieved — but this is the same unsanitized, no-CSP surface, reached from a file type where nothing signals that a diagram will be drawn. ## Impact Anyone with write access to a repository can make its pages display arbitrary full-screen content on the Gitea origin, with the real hostname and certificate, and make the underlying page unusable. Pushed to a shared repository, it affects every colleague who opens that repository, with no link sent and no unusual action taken — making fake session-expiry notices, credential-rotation instructions or outage banners credible because the instance itself serves them. Two bounds are worth stating explicitly: - **It does not cross a permission boundary.** The attacker needs write access to the repository holding the notebook; read-only access is not enough. Existing repository permissions are respected. - **The overlay is text.** The cell body passes through chroma, so there is no input, button or link. A credential prompt must end in 'go to this other host', which the victim types by hand. ## Remediation Upgrade to a fixed release. Until then, avoid rendering or serving untrusted `.ipynb` files (for example by disabling the Jupyter renderer on instances that accept notebooks from untrusted contributors). ## Reporter Toprak Yagcioglu. Found and reproduced against a local throwaway `gitea/gitea:1.27.1` container; nothing was tested against any third-party or production instance. Happy to supply a reproduction and to verify a candidate patch.

CVE-2026-60010.title: Repo-side team-link endpoint still bypasses RepoAdminChangeTeamAccess
CVE-2026-60010.description: ### Summary `PUT /api/v1/repos/{owner}/{repo}/teams/{team}` allows a non-owner repository admin to attach organization teams to a repository even when the organization has disabled that behaviour with `RepoAdminChangeTeamAccess=false`. An earlier advisory fixed the corresponding team-side endpoint; the repository-side endpoint retained the weaker check. ### Details The repository-side handler's exception relies on a repository permission check (`IsOwner()`), which for an organization repository is satisfied by a user promoted to owner-level access through an attached admin team. The fixed team-side endpoint instead checks actual organization ownership when `RepoAdminChangeTeamAccess` is disabled. The matching web collaboration-settings handler had the same weak check. ### Impact A user with delegated admin rights on one organization repository can grant other organization teams read or write access to that repository without approval from an actual organization owner, exposing private source and history and, for a write-capable team, granting push access. ### Affected versions Gitea `<= 1.27.2`. ### Patches Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39046, #39058). ### Workarounds None. Upgrade to 1.27.3.

CVE-2026-60021.title: Authenticated DoS in GitLab migration via uncancelable version probe
CVE-2026-60021.description: ### Summary The GitLab migration downloader probes the remote `/api/v4/version` endpoint using an HTTP client with no timeout, and issues that request without the migration task context. A malicious GitLab-compatible server can keep the response open indefinitely; because the request is not bound to the task context, task cancellation does not interrupt it. ### Details Subsequent GitLab API calls do pass the migration context; only the initial version probe does not. Reachable by any authenticated user who can start a repository migration. ### Impact Authenticated availability. An attacker who can start migrations against a server they control can hold migration workers open indefinitely, keep tasks running after cancellation, and exhaust the migration worker pool so other migrations remain queued. ### Affected versions Gitea `>= 1.16.0, <= 1.27.2`. ### Patches Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39023, #39035). ### Workarounds Restrict repository-migration permission to trusted users. Upgrade to 1.27.3.

CVE-2026-63792.title: Fork pull requests can read reusable workflow files from another private repository (missed sibling of GHSA-fj8v-hjwv-qm88)
CVE-2026-63792.description: ### Summary `CanReadWorkflowCrossRepo` decides whether an Actions run may read a reusable workflow file referenced from another repository. Its 'collaborative owner' branch grants cross-repository read through the collaborative-owner trust relationship without checking whether the run is a fork pull request. An earlier advisory fixed the same class of flaw in a sibling function but did not touch this one. ### Details A fork pull request opened against private repository A (no write access to A required) can read reusable workflow file contents of a different private repository B, at any git ref, provided A is private, B's Actions configuration lists A's owner as a collaborative owner (a normal use of the reusable-workflow sharing feature), and the fork pull request run is approved and runs. The workflow file path is confined to the configured workflow directories, but the git ref is caller-controlled. ### Impact Read-only disclosure of private reusable workflow file contents. No write access or code execution is granted by this issue. ### Affected versions Gitea `<= 1.27.2`. ### Patches Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39005, #39018). ### Workarounds None. Upgrade to 1.27.3.

CVE-2026-66874.title: A fork pull request author can satisfy a required Actions status check without any workflow running, because a filtered out workflow taken from the pull request HEAD posts a `skipped` commit status that counts as success
CVE-2026-66874.description: ### Summary Gitea writes a synthetic `skipped` commit status for a workflow that matched an event but was excluded by its own `branches:` or `paths:` filter, so that a required status check tied to that workflow does not block indefinitely. For a `pull_request` event the workflow definition is read from the pull request head commit, which for a fork pull request is controlled by the pull request author. The author can define a workflow whose name matches a required status check context and give it a filter that never matches, causing Gitea to write a `skipped` status under that context on the base repository. Because `skipped` counts as success when statuses are combined, the required check evaluates as passed. ### Details This path deliberately creates no workflow run, so the fork approval gate, which guards run creation, does not apply. No write access, runner or approval is required. The required context string is publicly visible as the check name on any pull request. ### Impact Bypass of branch-protection required status checks and of organization-mandated required workflows. Code can reach a protected branch with mandated checks shown as passing although nothing ran; where auto-merge is scheduled it can merge unattended. Any authenticated user who can fork and open a pull request is a potential actor. ### Affected versions Gitea `<= 1.27.2`. ### Patches Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39005, #39018). ### Workarounds None that preserve the protection. Upgrade to 1.27.3.

CVE-2026-70406.title: Public-only tokens can read private head repositories via compare and pull request creation (incomplete fix of CVE-2026-58443)
CVE-2026-70406.description: ### Summary The fix for CVE-2026-58443 added a 'token can access repository' check to `UpdatePullRequest` only. The shared helper `parseCompareInfo`, used by the compare-diff endpoint and by pull request creation, lacked the same check. A `public-only, read:repository` token can read commit history and diff content of a private head repository by routing the request through a public base repository. ### Details The route-level public-only middleware validates only the base repository named in the route. The head repository resolved inside `parseCompareInfo` is checked for user permission but not against the token's scope. Two entry points reach it: 1. `GET /api/v1/repos/{owner}/{repo}/compare/{basehead}` with `head` given as `owner/repo:branch`. The head repository does not need to be a fork of the base. 2. `POST /api/v1/repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls` with the same `head` syntax. Gitea then pushes the private head branch to `refs/pull/{index}/head` of the public base repository, where the public diff and patch endpoints serve it. The related disclosure of private head repository metadata and commit SHA through `ToAPIPullRequest` in the pull request read endpoints is handled separately in https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea/pull/39167. ### Impact Confidentiality bypass of the `public-only` token boundary. A leaked public-only token can read private repository commits and diffs it was explicitly restricted from. ### Affected versions Gitea `<= 1.27.2`. ### Patches Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 by https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea/pull/39006 and https://github.com/go-gitea/gitea/pull/39013. ### Workarounds None. Upgrade to 1.27.3.

CVE-2026-71301.title: Wiki-only members can read private pull request titles through markup preview
CVE-2026-71301.description: ### Summary In a private repository, a member with only Wiki access can use `POST /{owner}/{repo}/markup` to resolve a same-repository pull request reference and receive the pull request title and state icon, despite having no Issues or Pull Requests access. ### Details The markup route accepts any one of Code, Issues, Pull Requests, Releases or Wiki access. The renderer's unit check for referenced issues and pull requests is applied only in the cross-repository branch, so a same-repository reference reaches title and icon rendering without a unit check. No bodies, comments or attachments are returned. ### Impact Confidentiality. A Wiki-only member can read pull request titles and displayed state from a private repository. ### Affected versions Gitea `<= 1.27.2`. ### Patches Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39045, #39054). ### Workarounds None. Upgrade to 1.27.3.

CVE-2026-73130.title: Unbounded gitignores repository-creation field enables linear template-read amplification
CVE-2026-73130.description: ### Summary The `gitignores` field of the repository-creation form and API option struct has no maximum-length constraint. During repository initialization the field is split on commas and each name triggers a template read whose result is buffered in memory before `.gitignore` is written. A large attacker-controlled value therefore produces a proportional number of template reads and in-memory buffering. ### Details Reachable through `POST /repo/create` and `POST /api/v1/user/repos` (and the organization equivalent) when auto-init is enabled. ### Impact Uncontrolled resource consumption during repository creation, proportional to the submitted field length. Availability only. ### Affected versions Gitea `<= 1.27.2`. ### Patches Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39027, #39040). ### Workarounds None. Upgrade to 1.27.3.

CVE-2026-73273.title: Package size quota bypass and unbounded memory read in the Maven checksum upload path
CVE-2026-73273.description: ### Summary When a Maven artifact is uploaded with a checksum extension (`.md5`, `.sha1`, `.sha256`, `.sha512`), the handler reads the entire request body into memory and compares it to the stored digest, then returns — before the code path that enforces the package size quota. The checksum branch therefore has neither a size quota nor any bound on how much is read into memory, although a valid checksum value is at most 128 bytes. ### Details The body is read with `io.ReadAll` and copied again for the comparison; both allocations are sized by the client. The configured `LIMIT_SIZE_MAVEN` is not applied to this path. Reachable by any authenticated user with Maven package write access. ### Impact Package size-quota bypass and client-controlled memory allocation for a single request (uncontrolled resource consumption). A practical outage was not demonstrated; the issue should be read as an unbounded allocation and a quota bypass. ### Affected versions Gitea `<= 1.27.2`. ### Patches Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39028, #39031). ### Workarounds Limit request body size at the reverse proxy. Upgrade to 1.27.3.

CVE-2026-73504.title: Unauthenticated artifact-to-repository oracle in raw Actions downloads
CVE-2026-73504.description: ### Summary The raw Actions artifact download endpoint looks up the artifact row before validating the signed URL. Without authentication, an invalid signature produces one response when the supplied global artifact ID belongs to the named repository (and is upload-confirmed or expired) and a different response when it does not. Because artifact IDs are global auto-incrementing integers, this lets an unauthenticated caller test whether a guessed artifact ID belongs to an already-named private repository. ### Details The signature check still protects artifact bytes; only the ordering of the row lookup and the signature check creates the distinguishable responses. The endpoint does not reveal whether the repository exists, since inaccessible and nonexistent repositories return the same status. ### Impact Unauthenticated confirmation of the association between an artifact ID and a known private repository. Artifact contents are not exposed. ### Affected versions Gitea `<= 1.27.2`. ### Patches Fixed in Gitea 1.27.3 (#39049, #39053). ### Workarounds None. Upgrade to 1.27.3.

CVE-2026-73804.title: User-scoped tokens can mint unscoped HTTP signature API credentials
CVE-2026-73804.description: ### Summary Gitea allow a `write:user` token to create an SSH public key that then authenticates to the API through HTTP Signature without any API token scope. The vulnerable chain is: 1. A token with only `write:user` cannot directly call unrelated API categories such as `write:admin`. 2. The same token can call `POST /api/v1/user/keys` and add an attacker-controlled SSH public key to the token owner's account. 3. The matching private key can sign API requests through Gitea's HTTP Signature authentication. 4. `HTTPSign.Verify()` authenticates the request as the key owner and sets `IsApiToken=true`, but it does not set `ApiTokenScope`. 5. `tokenRequiresScopes()` skips route-level scope enforcement when `IsApiToken=true` but `ApiTokenScope` is absent. The result is a token-to-credential escalation. The attacker starts with a user-scoped token and ends with an unscoped API authentication method for the same account. The resulting access is still constrained by the account's normal Gitea RBAC, but it bypasses the API token scope boundary. ### Details The API auth group accepts HTTP Signature authentication for API routes: ```go // routers/api/v1/api.go:769-780 func buildAuthGroup() *auth.Group { group := auth.NewGroup( &auth.OAuth2{}, &auth.HTTPSign{}, &auth.Basic{}, // FIXME: this should be removed once we don't allow basic auth in API ) if setting.Service.EnableReverseProxyAuthAPI { group.Add(&auth.ReverseProxy{}) // TODO: does it still make sense to support reverse proxy auth in API? } // others: API doesn't support SSPI auth because the caller should use token return group } ``` When a request contains a valid HTTP Signature, Gitea resolves the SSH key owner and marks the request as API-token authenticated: ```go // services/auth/httpsign.go:39-86 // Verify extracts and validates HTTPsign from the Signature header of the request and returns // the corresponding user object on successful validation. // Returns nil if header is empty or validation fails. func (h *HTTPSign) Verify(req *http.Request, w http.ResponseWriter, store DataStore, sess SessionStore) (*user_model.User, error) { sigHead := req.Header.Get('Signature') if len(sigHead) == 0 { return nil, nil //nolint:nilnil // the auth method is not applicable } var ( publicKey *asymkey_model.PublicKey err error ) if len(req.Header.Get('X-Ssh-Certificate')) != 0 { // Handle Signature signed by SSH certificates if len(setting.SSH.TrustedUserCAKeys) == 0 { return nil, nil //nolint:nilnil // the auth method is not applicable } publicKey, err = VerifyCert(req) if err != nil { log.Debug('VerifyCert on request from %s: failed: %v', req.RemoteAddr, err) log.Warn('Failed authentication attempt from %s', req.RemoteAddr) return nil, nil //nolint:nilnil // the auth method is not applicable } } else { // Handle Signature signed by Public Key publicKey, err = VerifyPubKey(req) if err != nil { log.Debug('VerifyPubKey on request from %s: failed: %v', req.RemoteAddr, err) log.Warn('Failed authentication attempt from %s', req.RemoteAddr) return nil, nil //nolint:nilnil // the auth method is not applicable } } u, err := user_model.GetUserByID(req.Context(), publicKey.OwnerID) if err != nil { log.Error('GetUserByID: %v', err) return nil, err } store.GetData()['IsApiToken'] = true log.Trace('HTTP Sign: Logged in user %-v', u) return u, nil } ``` That path does not assign `ApiTokenScope`. The route-level scope middleware is fail-open for that state. It only checks required scopes when both `IsApiToken=true` and `ApiTokenScope` exists: ```go // routers/api/v1/api.go:319-363 func tokenRequiresScopes(requiredScopeCategories ...auth_model.AccessTokenScopeCategory) func(ctx *context.APIContext) { return func(ctx *context.APIContext) { // no scope required if len(requiredScopeCategories) == 0 { return } // Need OAuth2 token to be present. scope, scopeExists := ctx.Data['ApiTokenScope'].(auth_model.AccessTokenScope) if ctx.Data['IsApiToken'] != true || !scopeExists { return } // use the http method to determine the access level requiredScopeLevel := auth_model.Read if ctx.Req.Method == http.MethodPost || ctx.Req.Method == http.MethodPut || ctx.Req.Method == http.MethodPatch || ctx.Req.Method == http.MethodDelete { requiredScopeLevel = auth_model.Write } // get the required scope for the given access level and category requiredScopes := auth_model.GetRequiredScopes(requiredScopeLevel, requiredScopeCategories...) allow, err := scope.HasScope(requiredScopes...) if err != nil { ctx.APIError(http.StatusForbidden, 'checking scope failed: '+err.Error()) return } if !allow { ctx.APIError(http.StatusForbidden, fmt.Sprintf('token does not have at least one of required scope(s), required=%v, token scope=%v', requiredScopes, scope)) return } ctx.Data['requiredScopeCategories'] = requiredScopeCategories // check if scope only applies to public resources publicOnly, err := scope.PublicOnly() if err != nil { ctx.APIError(http.StatusForbidden, 'parsing public resource scope failed: '+err.Error()) return } // assign to true so that those searching should only filter public repositories/users/organizations ctx.PublicOnly = publicOnly } } ``` Therefore, a signed HTTP Signature request proceeds to the handler and normal account RBAC without checking `write:admin`, `write:repository`, `write:organization`, or other token categories. The key-enrollment route is available through the user scope group: ```go // routers/api/v1/api.go:1086-1091 m.Group('/keys', func() { m.Combo('').Get(user.ListMyPublicKeys). Post(bind(api.CreateKeyOption{}), user.CreatePublicKey) m.Combo('/{id}').Get(user.GetPublicKey). Delete(user.DeletePublicKey) }, rejectPublicOnly()) ``` `CreatePublicKey()` stores the supplied key for the authenticated user: ```go // routers/api/v1/user/key.go:202-249 func CreateUserPublicKey(ctx *context.APIContext, form api.CreateKeyOption, uid int64) { if user_model.IsFeatureDisabledWithLoginType(ctx.Doer, setting.UserFeatureManageSSHKeys) { ctx.APIErrorNotFound('Not Found', errors.New('ssh keys setting is not allowed to be visited')) return } content, err := asymkey_model.CheckPublicKeyString(form.Key) if err != nil { repo.HandleCheckKeyStringError(ctx, err) return } key, err := asymkey_model.AddPublicKey(ctx, uid, form.Title, content, 0, false) if err != nil { repo.HandleAddKeyError(ctx, err) return } apiLink := composePublicKeysAPILink() apiKey := convert.ToPublicKey(apiLink, key) if ctx.Doer.IsAdmin || ctx.Doer.ID == key.OwnerID { apiKey, _ = appendPrivateInformation(ctx, apiKey, key, ctx.Doer) } ctx.JSON(http.StatusCreated, apiKey) } // CreatePublicKey create one public key for me func CreatePublicKey(ctx *context.APIContext) { // swagger:operation POST /user/keys user userCurrentPostKey // --- // summary: Create a public key // consumes: // - application/json // produces: // - application/json // parameters: // - name: body // in: body // schema: // '$ref': '#/definitions/CreateKeyOption' // responses: // '201': // '$ref': '#/responses/PublicKey' // '422': // '$ref': '#/responses/validationError' form := web.GetForm(ctx).(*api.CreateKeyOption) CreateUserPublicKey(ctx, *form, ctx.Doer.ID) } ``` This means a `write:user` token can enroll an attacker-controlled key, and that key then becomes an unscoped HTTP Signature API credential. ### PoC ```http # Control: the original write:user token cannot directly use admin scope. POST /api/v1/admin/users Authorization: token {write-user-token} Content-Type: application/json {'username':'scope-control','email':'scope-control@example.invalid','password':'password','source_id':0,'login_name':'scope-control','send_notify':false,'must_change_password':false} # Expected: 403 Forbidden # Enroll an attacker-controlled SSH public key with the same write:user token. POST /api/v1/user/keys Authorization: token {write-user-token} Content-Type: application/json {'title':'httpsig-api-key','key':'ssh-rsa {attacker-public-key}'} # Expected: 201 Created # Sign an admin API request with the matching private key. The Signature keyId is # the SSH fingerprint of the enrolled public key, and the signed headers include # (request-target), (created), and (expires). POST /api/v1/admin/users Signature: keyId='{ssh-key-fingerprint}',algorithm='{ssh-signature-algorithm}',headers='(request-target) (created) (expires)',signature='{base64-signature}' Content-Type: application/json {'username':'created-by-httpsig','email':'created-by-httpsig@example.com','password':'password','source_id':0,'login_name':'created-by-httpsig','send_notify':false,'must_change_password':false} # Expected: 201 Created when the key owner is a site admin ``` ### Impact The attacker can enroll an SSH key and use HTTP Signature to reach any API category allowed by the victim account's normal RBAC. For a site-admin victim, the PoC shows access to `POST /api/v1/admin/users` without `write:admin`. For a non-admin victim, the same unscoped HTTP Signature credential can reach repository, package, organization, issue, or notification APIs according to the user's account permissions, without the corresponding token scopes. Destructive operations are also available where the victim account has the corresponding RBAC, such as repository/package deletion or admin-managed resource changes.

CVE-2026-78231.title: Unauthenticated Blind SSRF via OpenID Sign-In Verification
CVE-2026-78231.description: ### Summary When OpenID sign-in is enabled, Gitea accepts an unauthenticated GET request to `/user/login/openid` and passes attacker-controlled OpenID assertion parameters into the OpenID 2.0 verification flow. During verification, the upstream `github.com/yohcop/openid-go` library sends a server-side `POST` request to the attacker-controlled `openid.op_endpoint` URL using `http.DefaultClient`. This gives an unauthenticated remote attacker a blind SSRF primitive from the Gitea server. The attacker controls the destination URL and the form-encoded POST body. In deployments where the Gitea server can reach loopback, private-network, link-local, or otherwise internal HTTP services, this can be used to interact with services that are not directly reachable by the attacker. ### Details The vulnerable route is the OpenID sign-in endpoint: ```go m.Combo('/login/openid'). Get(auth.SignInOpenID). Post(web.Bind(forms.SignInOpenIDForm{}), auth.SignInOpenIDPost) ``` The route is gated by `openIDSignInEnabled`, but it does not require an authenticated user. When `[openid] ENABLE_OPENID_SIGNIN = true`, an anonymous client can reach the GET handler. ### Impact An attacker can cause the Gitea server to send an outbound HTTP POST request to an attacker-controlled URL by sending one unauthenticated GET request to `/user/login/openid`, provided OpenID sign-in is enabled. The attacker controls the target URL through `openid.op_endpoint` and controls much of the form-encoded body through the supplied OpenID query parameters. The impact depends on the deployment environment and network reachability. In common self-hosted deployments, Gitea may be able to reach services that are not exposed to the internet, including loopback services, internal admin panels, CI/CD endpoints, internal webhooks, private-network APIs, or link-local metadata endpoints. Because the response is not returned to the attacker, the primitive is blind, but it can still trigger state-changing actions on internal services that accept POST requests, and it can be used as an internal network interaction primitive. This also creates an availability risk if outbound requests can be made to slow or non-responsive targets, because the OpenID path uses the default HTTP client behavior without an apparent request timeout in this path. I would honestly argue that a higher environmental score may be appropriate where the Gitea server can reach sensitive unauthenticated internal services that accept form-encoded POST requests.
